claims.text: Factory's Droid scored 58.75% (reported as 58.8%) on Terminal-Bench, placing first among all agents on the leaderboard as of the September 25, 2025 write-up.
Factory agents occupy three of the top five Terminal-Bench positions: Droid with Opus 4.1 (no thinking) at 58.8%, GPT-5 (medium reasoning) at 52.5%, and Sonnet 4 (no thinking) at 50.5%.
Droid with Opus (58.8%) and Sonnet (50.5%) beats Claude Code with Opus (43.2%) on Terminal-Bench, and Droid with GPT-5 (52.5%) beats Codex CLI (42.8%).
Factory states that Droid with Sonnet outperforms all other agents using Opus on Terminal-Bench, and that agent framework can yield greater improvement than model selection.
Terminal-Bench Core (v0.1.1) consists of 80 human-verified, Dockerized, time-boxed tasks; a task counts as resolved only when all post-run tests pass, and the benchmark reports task-resolution rate.
Factory uses a three-tier prompting hierarchy: tool descriptions, system prompts, and system notifications (contextually injected user-level messages with time-sensitive guidance).

Factory designed system notifications because agentic models (notably Sonnet 3.7 and o3) show recency bias, prioritizing recent context over system-level instructions for low-level details over long trajectories; notifications enable rapid error recovery and task-specific adjustments.

Factory uses a modular architecture that shares core components while allowing model-specific adaptations, because providers' models differ, e.g. FIND_AND_REPLACE vs V4A diff file-editing formats and relative vs absolute path preferences.
Factory reports that tool reliability was the primary bottleneck for end-to-end task completion and adopted minimalist tool design principles.
Factory's platform targets enterprise organizations with 5,000-10,000+ engineers and aims to let droids take tasks from project-management tickets to mergeable pull requests.
Factory's planning approach uses subtask decomposition, e.g. separate plan steps for frontend, backend, tests, and feature-flag rollout.
Factory applies model predictive control to droids, continuously updating plans from environmental feedback during execution.
Factory uses explicit plan templates for certain task types, acknowledging a trade-off between rigidity (less creativity) and structure (more reliability).
Factory's droids ground themselves in the environment via AI-computer interfaces to existing development tools, observability systems, and knowledge bases.
The ZenML write-up notes the source is essentially a product pitch, so claims of 5-20x productivity gains and 50%+ task delegation targets need independent validation.

Factory integrates with Linear, Jira, Slack, GitHub, Sentry, and PagerDuty, plus memory and web search; in the demo only search is enabled initially and the Droid can request additional tools as it works.

In Factory's demo, a Droid searches the repository, summarizes findings, proposes a plan, and asks clarifying questions before execution, with an activity log and changing context panel during execution.

Factory's founders bet on the harness (integrations, information, execution, and feedback surrounding the model) rather than on model capability alone, and they leverage code's verifiability for feedback.
Factory's Missions feature has an orchestrator that breaks projects into milestones, spawns fresh worker sessions so no single agent is overloaded with context, and validates at every checkpoint.
Per the video description, the median Factory mission runs about 2 hours and 14% of missions run longer than a full day.

Missions use multi-model orchestration with different models in different roles, and a skill system that learns patterns from a specific codebase; the reviewer noted worker skills are created automatically and validation contract assertions are used.

A community guide recommends a Delegator (general purpose agent) that only reads, plans, delegates, and reviews structured reports and never writes code, with roles, tools, dependencies, and validation defined in AGENTS.md and custom Droids under ./factory/droids/.
The community guide describes a four-phase spec, test, implementation, verification flow, where sub-agent Droids do the work and the Delegator verifies outputs, with the run stopping when tests pass.
A review cites a 63.1% Terminal Bench score for Factory (December 2025) and notes that code quality still varies and requires solid review practices.
An independent review states it verified only public pages and docs, with no signed-in tests or coding benchmark, and that Factory's case is coordinating work rather than public proof of better code.
